title: Is Having Kids Worth It
intro: Chapter 18: Is Having Kids Worth It

tips.title: Start with the schemes the child is actually entitled to — India has no universal child benefit
tips.cost: The central schemes are free. A state scheme may have an income limit.
tips.inPlainWords: India does not pay a universal per-child cash benefit. The support is a patchwork: PM-JAY health cover for an eligible household, ICDS anganwadi services, PM POSHAN meals at school, the state maternity benefit, and some state child-benefit schemes. Check the eligibility and the local office. A private 'benefit agent' is not needed.
tips.benefit: Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY covers hospitalisation for eligible households. The Integrated Child Development Services provides supplementary nutrition and pre-school at an anganwadi. PM POSHAN provides a school meal. The Pradhan Mantri Matru Vandana Yojana provides a maternity benefit for an eligible woman. State governments run additional schemes, so the district social welfare office is the place to ask.
tips.sources: National Health Authority, PM-JAY. <https://nha.gov.in/>; Ministry of Women and Child Development, ICDS. <https://wcd.gov.in/>; Ministry of Education, PM POSHAN. <https://www.education.gov.in/>; Ministry of Rural Development. <https://rural.nic.in/>
tips.caveats: Eligibility is based on the SECC and state lists, not on a self-declaration. A scheme can change with the state government. Do not pay an agent to 'apply' for a free scheme.

tips.title: Maternity leave is 26 weeks for the first two children, and the employer pays the benefit
tips.cost: No cost to the employee. The employer pays the maternity benefit; where the woman is an insured person, the Employees' State Insurance Corporation pays it in place of the employer.
tips.inPlainWords: If your establishment is covered by Chapter VI of the Code on Social Security, 2020 (sections 59 to 72), in force from 21 November 2025, which replaced the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961, you get 26 weeks of paid maternity leave for the first two children, and 12 weeks after that. The leave may begin up to eight weeks before the expected date of delivery. A woman who adopts a child below three months of age, or who has a child through surrogacy, gets 12 weeks. The benefit is paid at your average daily wage for the days you actually worked in the three months before the leave. The employer may also let you work from home after the 26 weeks, on terms you both agree.
tips.benefit: Chapter VI also requires a crèche in every establishment with 50 or more employees, and two nursing breaks in addition to the usual interval until the child is 15 months old. You must give the employer notice of the leave and of the expected date of delivery. An employer cannot dismiss you, or cut your pay, because of the leave, and a woman who is dismissed can still claim the benefit she had earned.
tips.sources: Code on Social Security, 2020, Chapter VI (sections 59 to 72), in force from 21 November 2025, replacing the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961, Ministry of Labour and Employment. <https://labour.gov.in/>; Employees' State Insurance Corporation. <https://esic.gov.in/>; Ministry of Women and Child Development. <https://wcd.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: Chapter VI applies to every factory, mine or plantation, including one belonging to the Government, and to every shop or establishment in which ten or more employees are employed or were employed on any day of the preceding twelve months; the appropriate Government may notify other shops or establishments. If your workplace falls outside it, your protection comes from the state Shops and Establishments Act and your contract, so check both. A woman with two or more surviving children gets 12 weeks, not 26. Adoption in India runs through the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 and the Adoption Regulations, 2022. Keep the leave application, the delivery certificate and the salary slips.

tips.title: An employer cannot cut your pay or dismiss you because of pregnancy, childbirth or breastfeeding
tips.inPlainWords: Under the Code on Social Security, 2020 (Chapter VI) an employer cannot dismiss a woman, or reduce her pay, because she is on maternity leave or because of an absence caused by the pregnancy. A woman is also entitled to two nursing breaks, in addition to the usual rest interval, until the child is 15 months old. An employer that breaks Chapter VI can be prosecuted, and the penalty is imprisonment of up to six months, a fine of up to ₹50,000, or both (section 133).
tips.benefit: Chapter VI places the duty on the employer and gives a woman who is denied the benefit or the nursing breaks a route to complain to the Inspector-cum-Facilitator under section 72, who may direct the employer to pay the amount due or to withdraw a dismissal order, and to the labour authority of the state. A dismissal connected with maternity leave does not extinguish the benefit already earned. Keep the appointment letter, the salary slips, the leave application and any message about a transfer or a pay cut.
tips.sources: Code on Social Security, 2020, Chapter VI (sections 59 to 72), Ministry of Labour and Employment. <https://labour.gov.in/>; National Legal Services Authority. <https://nalsa.gov.in/>; Ministry of Women and Child Development. <https://wcd.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: Chapter VI applies to factories, mines, plantations and shops or establishments with ten or more employees; outside those, your protection comes from the state Shops and Establishments Act, the Industrial Relations Code, 2020 if you are a workman, or your contract. For a complaint, approach the Inspector-cum-Facilitator or the state labour department; for free legal aid, the National Legal Services Authority on 15100.

tips.title: The time-cost calculation is based on “whose time is being used,” not on “how hard it is”
tips.cost: There’s no monetary expense — only time is spent. For children under 3, that time is essentially taken up around the clock. The difficulty lies in the fact that this happens daily, not just for a few tough days.
tips.inPlainWords: Count up all the hours spent caring for the child each day, plus every nighttime wake-up call. Then multiply that total by the hourly wage of the person doing the work. The resulting figure is usually far higher than the cost of formula and diapers. That’s why it’s best to discuss how responsibilities will be divided before having a child.
tips.benefit: By converting daily childcare time and nighttime interruptions into hours, then multiplying by the caregiver’s hourly wage, you arrive at a number that typically exceeds the cost of formula and diapers. Even unpaid tasks like childcare, cooking, and nightly wake-ups should be treated the same way — converted to hours and multiplied by a wage figure to be included in the total cost. The calculation method mirrors that used in Section 10 for household chores. Having a clear division of labor agreed upon beforehand makes it easier to decide whether to have a child.
tips.sources: Author’s experience, no direct literature; see Section 10 for caliber; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. <https://mohfw.gov.in/>; Ministry of Women and Child Development. <https://wcd.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: The goal isn’t to produce a perfectly accurate figure. Rather, it’s to ensure both partners discuss responsibilities using the same calculation framework prior to having a child, rather than arguing about it afterward.

tips.title: Breaking down costs into three periods: ages 0–3, compulsory education, and post‑compulsory education
tips.cost: There’s no single fixed figure for total expenses; they vary widely depending on the city and the approach families take. The real challenge is to carefully separate the costs into these three periods instead of guessing a rough total.
tips.inPlainWords: For ages 0–3, most spending goes toward childcare arrangements — whether parents care for the child themselves, grandparents help out, or a professional is hired. During primary and middle school, the main expenses are housing and extracurricular activities. After that, costs center on further education pathways. Since spending patterns differ so much in each phase, lumping them together yields only an intimidating overall figure.
tips.benefit: The bulk of expenses in the 0–3 age range relate to childcare methods; for compulsory education, housing and after‑school programs dominate; later on, costs shift toward higher‑level schooling. Because these categories are distinct, mixing them obscures the true financial picture.
tips.sources: author’s experience, no direct literature; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. <https://mohfw.gov.in/>; Ministry of Women and Child Development. <https://wcd.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: Break the cost into three periods: ages 0–3 (delivery, immunisation, childcare), the school years (fees, books, transport, PM POSHAN covers a midday meal at a government school), and after 18 (college or training, where a scholarship or an education loan may apply). Add the cost of health cover; PM-JAY covers an eligible household. A private school and a government school differ by an order of magnitude, so compare the actual fee structure, not an average.

tips.title: Keep separate accounts for having kids for your elders, for marriage, and for old-age security
tips.cost: There’s no monetary cost — only the cost of having a sincere conversation. The real challenge is speaking openly about these topics without dodging them.
tips.inPlainWords: Others may expect you to have children, and that can certainly be one factor to consider. Yet the time and money involved are expenses you personally bear. “Relying on kids for old-age support” deserves its own separate calculation, since it hinges on another person’s financial capacity and willingness two decades down the line. Be sure to also write down the consequences of choosing not to have kids, so you can compare both sides fairly.
tips.benefit: The reasoning here mirrors that in Section 10. External expectations are valid considerations, but their associated costs must be recorded on your own ledger, not someone else’s. This is especially true for “relying on kids for old-age support,” which depends entirely on another individual’s future financial situation and willingness to help.
tips.sources: Author’s experience, no direct literature; see Section 10 for similar analysis; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. <https://mohfw.gov.in/>; Ministry of Women and Child Development. <https://wcd.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: Make sure to list both the consequences of having kids and those of not having them, then compare them side by side. Recording only one side of the equation doesn’t truly qualify as keeping accounts at all.

tips.title: When considering delaying childbirth, factor female age into the life balance sheet: spontaneous conception odds and IVF success rates decline sharply around age 40
tips.cost: Zero financial outlay; requires an honest, objective conversation between partners. The difficulty is integrating biological reproductive windows with career milestones, savings targets, and mortgage timelines rather than indefinitely postponing family planning.
tips.inPlainWords: Female biological fecundability declines progressively with age; women in their early 40s have roughly half the monthly conception rate of women in their early 30s. Spontaneous miscarriage rates also rise, reaching about one-third of pregnancies between ages 40 and 44. In vitro fertilization (IVF) cannot fully overcome ovarian aging: at ages 43 to 44, only about 5% of embryo transfers result in a live birth.
tips.benefit: In natural fecundability, a prospective cohort study of women aged 30–44 without history of infertility demonstrated that compared to women aged 30–31, monthly conception probability was 53% lower at ages 40–41 (fecundability ratio 0.47, 95% CI: 0.28–0.78) and 59% lower at ages 42–44 (ratio 0.39, 95% CI: 0.16–0.93); at ages 38–39, conception was 30% lower (ratio 0.70, 95% CI: 0.48–1.01), while ages 32–33 showed no difference compared to 30–31. Nulligravid women had lower fecundability across all ages. In a Danish general population cohort, women aged 35–40 had a conception ratio of 0.77 compared to ages 20–24, whereas male age had a much smaller impact (ratio 0.95 at ages 35–39). In spontaneous pregnancy loss, a Norwegian nationwide registry study of ~420,000 pregnancies found the lowest miscarriage risk at ages 25–29 (9.8%), rising to 10.8% at 30–34, 16.7% at 35–39, 32.2% at 40–44, and 53.6% past age 45. In embryonic genetics, comprehensive chromosomal screening of 15,169 consecutive IVF trophectoderm biopsies revealed that embryonic aneuploidy rates rise steadily with maternal age past 26: while 2% to 6% of cycles between ages 26 and 37 produce all-aneuploid embryos, this jumps to 33% at age 42 and 53% at age 44. In assisted reproductive outcomes, preliminary UK Human Fertilisation and Embryology Authority (HFEA 2022) data showed live birth rates per fresh autologous embryo transfer of 35% for ages 18–34, 26% for 35–37, 18% for 38–39, 10% for 40–42, and 5% for 43–44. Regulatory context in India: the Assisted Reproductive Technology (Regulation) Act, 2021 and the rules made under it govern ART clinics and banks. Treatment is open to married couples and to single women, within the age limits in the Act, and a clinic must be registered and follow its conditions. ART clinics must also follow the Pre-conception and Pre-natal Diagnostic Techniques (Prohibition of Sex Selection) Act, 1994, which prohibits prenatal sex determination.
tips.sources: Steiner AZ, Jukic AM (2016). Impact of female age and nulligravidity on fecundity in an older reproductive age cohort. Fertility and Sterility, 105(6), 1584-1588. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fertnstert.2016.02.028>; Rothman KJ, et al. (2013). Volitional determinants and age-related decline in fecundability: a general population prospective cohort study in Denmark. Fertility and Sterility, 99(7), 1958-1964. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fertnstert.2013.02.040>; Magnus MC, et al. (2019). Role of maternal age and pregnancy history in risk of miscarriage: prospective register based study. BMJ, 364, l869. <https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.l869>; Franasiak JM, et al. (2014). The nature of aneuploidy with increasing age of the female partner: a review of 15,169 consecutive trophectoderm biopsies. Fertility and Sterility, 101(3), 656-663. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fertnstert.2013.11.004>; Human Fertilisation and Embryology Authority (2024). Fertility Treatment 2022: Preliminary Trends and Figures. <https://www.hfea.gov.uk/about-us/publications/research-and-data/fertility-treatment-2022-preliminary-trends-and-figures/>; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. Assisted Reproductive Technology (Regulation) Act, 2021 and the Assisted Reproductive Technology (Regulation) Rules, 2022. <https://mohfw.gov.in/>; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. Pre-conception and Pre-natal Diagnostic Techniques (Prohibition of Sex Selection) Act, 1994. <https://mohfw.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: This analysis does not advocate any specific childbearing age, but presents empirical reproductive biological realities to weigh alongside financial costs (Chapter 18, Item 5) and parental time investments (Chapter 18, Item 4). Statistics represent population-wide averages; consult reproductive specialists for individualized ovarian reserve assessment (e.g. AMH and antral follicle counts). Public schemes generally do not cover ART, and a private policy usually excludes it, so ask the clinic for its schedule of charges and check your own policy before you start. Preconception preparations and folic acid supplementation are covered in Chapter 27, Item 1.
